title: Growth, inflation and real return
blurb: The Rule of 72, growing prices and what your money really earns.

levels.title: The Rule of 72 and where it is rough
learn: Use the Rule of 72 forwards and backwards.
Say where the rule is close to the exact time and where it is rough.

cards.text: The Rule of 72 estimates how long money takes to double: years = 72 divided by the yearly rate. At 6% that is 72 / 6 = 12 years. It also runs backwards. Money that doubled in 6 years grew at about 72 / 6 = 12% a year. The rule is for one lump of money with nothing added or taken out.

One guess is 100 / 6, about 17 years, as if every year added 6% of the first $10,000. But year two’s interest is on a bigger balance, so the wait is shorter. Here is $10,000 at 6%, multiplied by 1.06 each year, to the nearest dollar. It passes $20,000 in year 12.
The exact doubling time at 6% is a little under 12 years: about 11.9. A calculator or spreadsheet finds it. The rule says 12, a very close estimate. Here are both at six example rates, in years.

Read the gap. At 6%, 9% and 12% the rule is within about 0.1 of a year. At 1% it says 72 years, but the exact time is 69.7, about 2 years too long. At 24% it says 3 years and the exact time is 3.2, a little too short. At very low or very high rates, treat the rule as rougher.

Interest is not always added once a year. Say 6% a year is added monthly: 0.5% each month, 144 months in 12 years. $10,000 grows to 10,000 x 1.005^144 = $20,508, a bit more than $20,000. Doubling takes about 11.6 years, not 12. The rule is still a good first check.

levels.title: Growing with regular deposits
learn: Follow a balance month by month when deposits go in.
Use the shortcut and see what a bigger deposit, rate or time does.

cards.text: Most people add money every month. Each month the balance grows by that month’s interest, then the deposit goes in at the end of the month. At 6% a year the monthly rate is 6% divided by 12, which is 0.5%, so the balance is multiplied by 1.005. Here are the first three months of $100 deposits.

Do this 120 times and you have ten years of $100 deposits. You put in $12,000 and the balance is $16,388. The rest, $4,388, is interest. The longer it runs, the bigger the interest share. A spreadsheet’s future value function adds up the chain for you.

A shortcut saves 120 steps. Balance = deposit x (1.005^n - 1) / 0.005, where n is the number of months and 0.005 is the monthly rate. Two slips to avoid: typing 6% where 0.5% a month belongs, and typing 10 for n when ten years is 120 months. Rates here are examples.

A lump sum and monthly deposits can be added together. Start with $10,000 and add $100 a month for 12 years at 6%. The lump grows alone, the deposits grow alone, and the two add up. The Rule of 72 describes only the lump: it knows nothing about the money you add later.

What helps most: a bigger deposit, a higher rate or more years? Here are three plans for 20 years of saving. A higher deposit and a higher rate both help. So does time, because it lets interest earn interest for longer. These rates are examples, not forecasts.

levels.title: Inflation grows your costs
learn: Grow a bill to a later year at an example inflation rate.
Compare costs and income in the same year’s dollars.

cards.text: Inflation is a rise in prices over time, so the same bills cost more. Costs grow the way money does: each year you multiply by 1 plus the rate. Take Mia’s bills, $3,000 a month today. If prices rise 2% a year (an example rate), next year they are $3,000 x 1.02 = $3,060.00.

Over 33 years you multiply by 1.02 thirty-three times. That is 1.02^33, about 1.92. Mia’s $3,000 of bills becomes $5,766.69 a month. A common slip is to add 2% thirty-three times, which is 66%, and get $4,980.00. That misses that each rise is on prices that already rose.

One point of inflation changes the answer a lot. Here is the same $3,000 a month after 33 years at three example rates. A small difference in rate, repeated for many years, becomes a large difference in dollars.

The Rule of 72 works on prices too: divide 72 by the inflation rate. At 2%, prices double in about 72 / 2 = 36 years. The Bank of Canada aims to keep inflation near 2%, the midpoint of a range from 1% to 3%. That is its target.

Costs and income must be compared in the same year’s dollars. Mia expects $4,500 a month in 33 years. That is more than $3,000, so it looks safe. But her bills will be $5,766.69 by then, which is $1,266.69 more than her income.

levels.title: Real return
learn: Work out a real return and say what a statement really buys.
Use the Rule of 72 on the real return.

cards.text: A statement counts dollars. That is the nominal amount. Real means what the money buys after prices rise. Take $200,000 in a GIC at 3% for 10 years, with prices rising 3% a year (a class example). The statement grows to $268,783. Prices grew just as much, so it still buys only $200,000 of today’s goods.

Real return = (1 + rate) / (1 + inflation) - 1. At a 3% rate and 3% inflation that is 1.03 / 1.03 - 1 = 0, so you run in place. Dollars on the statement divided by (1 + inflation) for each year gives what they buy today. Here is the same GIC at three inflation rates.

A shortcut is rate minus inflation: 3% - 5% = -2%, near the exact -1.9%. It drifts at bigger rates: at 8% and 5% it says 3.0%, but the exact answer is 2.9%. The game shows both numbers: the Bank of DAA lists a savings rate and the inflation rate. The game starts at 2.75% and 2.1%, and the teacher can change them.

The Rule of 72 can run on the real return. A 6% fund with 2% inflation has a real return of about 4%, so what it buys doubles in about 72 / 4 = 18 years. The dollars double sooner, in about 12 years, but each dollar buys less by then. Doubled dollars are not doubled buying power.

levels.title: Percent change and short stretches
learn: Find a percent change and a new price from one.
Say why a short stretch is only a sample.

cards.text: Percent change says how far a price moved as a share of where it started: (latest - start) / start x 100. A price goes from $50.00 to $56.00. The change is $6.00, and $6.00 / $50.00 = 0.12, which is 12%. A fall is the same sum with a minus sign. Divide by the start, not the latest.

You can run it the other way. A $60.00 price that rises 10% gains $6.00 and becomes $66.00. One that falls 10% loses $6.00 and becomes $54.00. A rise of 10% and then a fall of 10% does not get you back: $66.00 x 0.90 = $59.40, because the fall is 10% of a bigger price.

A percent change covers whatever stretch you measure. A price that goes from $1,000.00 to $1,300.00 over 4 years has changed 30% in total. That is not 30% a year. Always say how long the stretch was before you compare two changes.

A short stretch is a sample, not a verdict. Here is a made-up price that starts at $50.00. After week 2 it is up 8% from the start. After week 4 it is down 5% from the start. After week 6 it is up 4% from the start. Stop on a different week and you tell a different story.
